AI: Artificial intelligence: computer systems performing tasks such as prediction, language understanding or planning; this label does not imply human judgment or reliability.
API: Application programming interface: the operations, input/output shapes and error contract one component exposes to another.
ML: Machine learning: fitting model behavior from data rather than specifying every decision as a rule.
DL: Deep learning: machine learning using neural networks with multiple learned transformations.
NLP: Natural language processing: methods for analyzing or generating human language.
GenAI: Generative artificial intelligence: models that generate outputs such as text, images or audio from learned distributions.
LLM: Large language model: a model trained on large language datasets, commonly used to predict and generate tokens.
RAG: Retrieval-augmented generation: finding external evidence and supplying it to a generator when answering a question.
HTTP: Hypertext Transfer Protocol: request/response rules for transferring representations between clients and servers.
HTTPS: HTTP Secure: HTTP carried over a TLS-encrypted, authenticated connection.
TLS: Transport Layer Security: the protocol that encrypts traffic and authenticates the remote endpoint when certificates are validated correctly.
TCP: Transmission Control Protocol: a reliable ordered byte-stream transport; it does not preserve application message boundaries.
UDP: User Datagram Protocol: a datagram transport without built-in delivery or ordering guarantees.
DNS: Domain Name System: the distributed system that resolves names to records such as server addresses.
IP: Internet Protocol: addressing and packet routing across networks.
URL: Uniform Resource Locator: an address identifying a resource and how to access it.
URI: Uniform Resource Identifier: a string identifying a resource; a URL is one kind of URI.
JSON: JavaScript Object Notation: a text data format with objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null; parsing does not validate business rules.
JSONB: Binary JSON representation in PostgreSQL: an indexed, decomposed storage format for JSON data; it does not replace relational constraints.
HTML: Hypertext Markup Language: the document structure and semantic elements presented by a browser.
CSS: Cascading Style Sheets: rules controlling document presentation, layout and responsive behavior.
JS: JavaScript: the programming language commonly used to implement browser behavior and server applications.
DOM: Document Object Model: the browser's programmable tree of document nodes.
UI: User interface: the controls and content through which a person interacts with a system.
UX: User experience: the person's overall interaction, including clarity, latency, errors and accessibility.
ARIA: Accessible Rich Internet Applications: attributes describing interface roles and states to assistive technology; native semantics are preferable when available.
WCAG: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines: accessibility criteria used to assess how people with disabilities can perceive and operate web content.
WAI: Web Accessibility Initiative: the W3C effort providing accessibility standards and guidance.
W3C: World Wide Web Consortium: the organization developing many web standards.
CORS: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing: browser-enforced rules governing whether script can read responses from another origin; it is not authentication.
CSRF: Cross-Site Request Forgery: inducing a victim's browser to send an unwanted authenticated request using automatically attached credentials.
XSS: Cross-Site Scripting: attacker-controlled content executing as script in another user's application origin.
SSRF: Server-Side Request Forgery: tricking a server into fetching an attacker-chosen destination, potentially reaching private services.
JWT: JSON Web Token: a token format carrying claims; signature, algorithm, issuer, audience and validity checks are still required.
OAuth: OAuth authorization framework: delegated access using scoped tokens; it is not itself a user identity protocol.
OIDC: OpenID Connect: an identity layer on OAuth 2.0 for authenticating users and communicating identity claims.
PKCE: Proof Key for Code Exchange: binds an authorization-code exchange to a verifier to reduce code-interception risk.
RBAC: Role-based access control: granting permissions through roles assigned to principals.
ABAC: Attribute-based access control: deciding permissions using principal, resource, action and environment attributes.
ACL: Access control list: permissions attached to a resource specifying which principals may perform which actions.
RLS: Row-level security: database policies restricting which rows a role may read or modify.
SQL: Structured Query Language: the language used to define, query and modify relational data.
DDL: Data definition language: SQL statements defining or changing structures such as tables and indexes.
ORM: Object-relational mapper: a library mapping objects and relationships to relational queries and rows.
UUID: Universally unique identifier: a large identifier designed to make independently generated collisions extremely unlikely; it is not an authorization secret.
ID: Identifier: a value naming an entity, event or operation; its uniqueness scope must be specified.
ACID: Atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability: transaction properties concerning all-or-nothing changes, valid state, concurrent behavior and committed persistence.
MVCC: Multiversion concurrency control: keeping row versions so reads and writes can coordinate without every read blocking every write.
WAL: Write-ahead log: recording changes durably before their data pages so recovery can replay committed work.
CPU: Central processing unit: a general-purpose processor executing program instructions.
GPU: Graphics processing unit: a processor suited to parallel tensor and other throughput-oriented workloads.
RAM: Random-access memory: working memory used while processes execute; it is normally volatile.
I/O: Input/output: exchanging data with files, devices or networks, often involving waits outside CPU computation.
GIL: Global interpreter lock: in conventional CPython builds, a lock restricting concurrent Python-bytecode execution; build mode and native extensions matter.
IPC: Interprocess communication: mechanisms for exchanging data or signals between separate processes.
OS: Operating system: software managing processes, memory, storage, scheduling and devices.
LRU: Least recently used: an eviction policy removing entries whose last use is oldest.
TTL: Time to live: an expiry duration; it limits retention but does not by itself enforce freshness or revocation.
ETL: Extract, transform, load: transforming source data before loading it into the target analytical system.
ELT: Extract, load, transform: loading raw data first and transforming within the destination environment.
CDC: Change data capture: reading inserts, updates and deletions from a source change stream for incremental replication.
DLQ: Dead-letter queue: a separate destination for records that cannot be processed under the retry policy and need inspection or repair.
SSE: Server-sent events: a UTF-8, line-framed HTTP event stream from server to client.
NDJSON: Newline-delimited JSON: independent JSON documents separated by newline delimiters; network reads need not align with records.
UTF-8: Unicode Transformation Format, 8-bit: a variable-length encoding of Unicode characters; byte chunks can split a character.
ASCII: American Standard Code for Information Interchange: a 7-bit character encoding for basic Latin characters and controls.
SDK: Software development kit: client libraries and supporting tools implementing a service or protocol interface.
STDIO: Standard input/output: process streams used as a local transport, with protocol output kept separate from diagnostic logs.
MCP: Model Context Protocol: a negotiated protocol connecting AI applications to tools, resources and prompts.
A2A: Agent-to-Agent protocol: a protocol for discovering and delegating work to remote agent services through task and message contracts.
ADK: Agent Development Kit: the agent framework discussed in this course; framework behavior depends on the pinned SDK version.
ANN: Approximate nearest neighbor: similarity search trading some exact-neighbor recall for faster or more scalable retrieval.
HNSW: Hierarchical Navigable Small World: a graph-based approximate-neighbor index with connectivity, search and memory trade-offs.
IVF: Inverted file index: approximate search that first selects clusters and then searches their assigned vectors.
BM25: Best Matching 25: a lexical retrieval scoring family using term rarity, frequency saturation and document-length normalization.
TF-IDF: Term frequency–inverse document frequency: weighting words by occurrence in a document and rarity across the corpus.
RRF: Reciprocal rank fusion: combining ranked lists using reciprocal rank contributions instead of comparing their raw scores.
MRR: Mean reciprocal rank: the mean of one divided by the rank of the first relevant result, with zero for a missing hit.
NDCG: Normalized discounted cumulative gain: a ranking metric comparing discounted graded relevance with the best ordering.
nDCG: Normalized discounted cumulative gain: a ranking metric rewarding highly relevant results near the top relative to an ideal order.
OCR: Optical character recognition: converting text in images into machine-readable characters; it does not guarantee correct reading order or meaning.
PDF: Portable Document Format: a page-oriented document format whose visual layout may not provide a usable semantic text order.
ASR: Automatic speech recognition: converting spoken audio into recognized language text.
STT: Speech to text: converting audio speech into text, commonly implemented using ASR models.
TTS: Text to speech: synthesizing spoken audio from text.
VAD: Voice activity detection: deciding which audio regions contain speech; it does not establish speaker identity or intent.
WER: Word error rate: substitutions, deletions and insertions divided by reference word count in a transcript comparison.
CNN: Convolutional neural network: a neural architecture using shared local filters, often for spatial signals.
RNN: Recurrent neural network: a neural architecture carrying state through sequential inputs.
LSTM: Long short-term memory: a gated recurrent neural network architecture designed to retain useful information over sequences.
SGD: Stochastic gradient descent: updating parameters using gradients estimated from samples or minibatches.
MSE: Mean squared error: the average squared prediction residual used as a regression loss or evaluation measure.
MAE: Mean absolute error: the average absolute prediction residual, less sensitive to large errors than squared loss.
PCA: Principal component analysis: finding orthogonal directions of high variance in centered data for a lower-dimensional representation.
SVD: Singular value decomposition: factorizing a matrix into left directions, singular values and right directions.
AUC: Area under a curve: a summary whose meaning depends on the named curve, such as ROC or precision–recall.
ROC: Receiver operating characteristic: the trade-off between true-positive and false-positive rates across thresholds.
PR: Precision–recall in model metrics; pull request in source-control workflow. Interpret the abbreviation from its surrounding context.
BPE: Byte-pair encoding: a subword tokenization approach built by merging frequent symbol pairs.
KV: Key/value: in transformer inference, cached attention keys and values for previously processed tokens.
LoRA: Low-rank adaptation: learning low-rank parameter updates while freezing selected base-model weights.
QLoRA: Quantized low-rank adaptation: training low-rank adapters while keeping a quantized frozen base model.
PEFT: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning: adaptation methods training a relatively small subset or addition of model parameters.
SFT: Supervised fine-tuning: training on labeled input/output examples to adapt model behavior.
DPO: Direct preference optimization: fitting a model to preference pairs through a preference objective relative to a reference policy.
RLHF: Reinforcement learning from human feedback: using human preferences to inform a reward signal and optimize model behavior.
KL: Kullback–Leibler divergence: a directional measure of how one probability distribution differs from another; it is not a symmetric distance.
L2: Euclidean norm or squared-norm regularization, depending on context: the square root of summed squared coordinates, or a penalty built from them.
L1: Sum-of-absolute-values norm, or a regularization penalty using it; the context determines whether a norm or penalty is meant.
REST: Representational State Transfer: an architectural style for resource interactions, commonly implemented using HTTP.
CRUD: Create, read, update and delete: basic operations on persistent entities.
CI: Continuous integration: automated checks validating changes as they are integrated into a shared repository.
CD: Continuous delivery or deployment: automating release preparation or production release; specify which policy is intended.
MLOps: Machine learning operations: practices for versioning, releasing, monitoring and maintaining data and model systems.
SLO: Service-level objective: a target for a measured service indicator over a specified window.
SLI: Service-level indicator: the actual measurement used to assess service behavior, such as successful requests or latency.
SLA: Service-level agreement: an agreement defining service commitments and consequences, distinct from an internal SLO.
RPO: Recovery point objective: the maximum acceptable age of lost data after recovery.
RTO: Recovery time objective: the maximum acceptable time to restore the required service.
P95: 95th percentile: a value at or below which 95 percent of the observed sample falls; define the sample and measurement window.
p95: 95th percentile: a tail measure of the observed sample, such as end-to-end latency.
p99: 99th percentile: a more extreme tail measure; its reliability depends on the number and representativeness of observations.
PII: Personally identifiable information: information that can identify a person directly or in combination with other data.
ADR: Architecture decision record: a written decision with context, alternatives and consequences.
FAQ: Frequently asked questions: a collection of recurring questions and answers.
FAISS: Facebook AI Similarity Search: a vector-search library; it is not a complete database or authorization layer.
NIST: National Institute of Standards and Technology: a US standards and measurement organization, including security and AI risk guidance.
UTC: Coordinated Universal Time: the common reference time scale used for timestamps; business-local calendar rules may still need a named time zone.
FIFO: First in, first out: a queue policy serving earlier enqueued items before later ones.
BFS: Breadth-first search: graph traversal exploring nodes in layers of increasing edge distance.
DFS: Depth-first search: graph traversal exploring a branch before backtracking.
CLI: Command-line interface: a program interface driven through arguments, streams and exit status.
PCM: Pulse-code modulation: representing audio samples as numerical amplitudes under a sample-rate and encoding contract.
F1: F1 score: the harmonic mean of precision and recall; it is a metric name, not an acronym expansion.
HR: Human resources: the organizational function referenced by a source or business-policy context.
ETag: Entity tag: an HTTP representation validator used in conditional requests; it does not itself enforce permissions.
ReAct: Reasoning and acting: a pattern alternating model reasoning or decisions with environment/tool actions under a bounded execution policy.
HyDE: Hypothetical document embeddings: generating a hypothetical answer-like document to help construct a retrieval representation; generated text is not verified evidence.
GraphRAG: Graph-based retrieval-augmented generation: using entity/relationship structure or graph-derived context in evidence retrieval and answer synthesis.
WebRTC: Web Real-Time Communication: browser APIs and protocols for realtime audio, video and data connections under an explicit signaling and network policy.
ReLU: Rectified linear unit: an activation returning zero for negative input and the input for positive input.
DB: Database: a system storing and querying data under a defined integrity, concurrency and durability contract.
SVM: Support vector machine: a margin-based learned decision method, optionally using a kernel.
kNN: k-nearest neighbors: predicting from selected nearby reference examples under a chosen representation and distance.
RL: Reinforcement learning: learning a policy from rewards for actions in an environment, often with delayed consequences.
TP: True positive: an actually positive example classified as positive under the declared label and threshold.
FP: False positive: an actually negative example classified as positive.
FN: False negative: an actually positive example classified as negative.
TN: True negative: an actually negative example classified as negative.
